turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Totally, let’s keep it really simple.

1. What you can buy from us

Roses
This is our main thing.

Grown on their own roots in 1‑gallon containers with soil (not bare root).
Come in different styles, for example:
Big classic roses (great for cutting and vases)
Climbing roses (to grow over arches, fences, or trellises)
Bush/shrub roses (nice full plants for beds and borders)

Perennials
These are plants that come back every year, like lavender, hosta, hydrangea, etc. Good for filling in around roses so your garden looks full, not just roses on their own.

Bulbs
These are things like tulips, daffodils, alliums, and irises.

Planted mostly in fall.
They sleep underground and pop up in spring.
We also sell some potted tulips and daffodils in spring that are already growing in containers.

Soil amendments & fertilizers
These are “food and improvements” for your soil:

Soil amendments (mint compost, worm castings, cow manure, living soil, bone meal) help make your soil richer and better structured.
Fertilizers (OmniMeal, Founders Fish Fertilizer, Boost & Bloom) give your plants nutrients so they grow and bloom better.
2. Where they can grow

Two simple ideas to know:

Sun

Full sun: needs 6+ hours of direct sun per day. Most roses fall here.
Partial shade: can do okay with about 4+ hours and some shade.

Hardiness zone
This is how cold your area gets in winter and which plants will survive.
At the top of our website, you can pick your zone, and the site will show plants that are suited to your area.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Great question, and it’s smart to think about using everything correctly from the start.

Below is a simple first‑time guide assuming you have a new rose and the Get Growing Bundle (cow manure, bone meal, mint compost, Founders Fish Fertilizer).

If you’re planting in the ground

Dig the hole
About 2 ft wide and 2 ft deep, in a spot with at least 6 hours of sun.

Prepare the bottom of the hole

Put about 3 inches of your regular garden soil back into the bottom.

Mix your amendments with soil
In a wheelbarrow or bucket, mix:

Garden soil
A few shovels of cow manure
About 1 cup of bone meal
Some mint compost (up to one small 1.5‑quart bag per plant)

Plant the rose

Place the rose in the hole at the right height (the base of the plant just below soil level).
Backfill around it with your soil + amendments mix.
Gently press the soil to remove big air pockets, but do not stomp hard.

Water with fish fertilizer

Mix 4 oz of Founders Fish Fertilizer per 1 gallon of water.
1 gallon of this mix usually feeds 2–3 roses.
Pour the solution on the soil around the roots, not on the leaves.
This counts as your first deep watering.

After planting

Keep the soil evenly moist (not soggy) while the rose is getting established.
Repeat the fish fertilizer every 4–6 weeks in the growing season.
If you’re planting in a container

Choose a pot
At least 2 ft wide with a drainage hole.

Mix the potting soil
In a bucket or the pot itself, mix:

Good quality potting soil (without granular/time‑release fertilizer)
Some cow manure
About 1 cup of bone meal

Plant the rose

Fill the bottom of the pot with your mix.
Set the rose in, then fill around it with more mix to the final level.
Press gently to settle the soil.

Top dress with mint compost

Spread mint compost on top of the soil around the base of the plant.
This helps hold moisture and protect roots.

Water with fish fertilizer

Mix 4 oz of Founders Fish Fertilizer per 1 gallon of water.
Water slowly around the base of the plant until water runs from the drainage hole.
Repeat every 3–4 weeks during the growing season.
A couple of “do this, not that” tips
Apply fish fertilizer to the soil only, not on the leaves.
Do not use a potting mix that already has strong granular or time‑release fertilizer for a young rose.
Keep your rose outdoors in full sun.
